title: Skip Neighbours
statement:
A street has several stalls in a row, and stall `i` gives a prize worth `prizes[i]` coins. A rule says you may **not take prizes from two stalls that are next to each other**.

Return the **most coins** you can collect.

examples.explanation: Take the two 5s at the ends.

hints.nudge: Look at the last stall. If you take it, what can you say about the stall before it? If you skip it?
hints.pattern: Dynamic programming over the stalls: best(i) depends only on best(i-1) and best(i-2).
hints.pseudocode:
prev2 = 0; prev1 = 0
for each p in prizes:
  current = max(prev1, prev2 + p)
  prev2 = prev1; prev1 = current
return prev1
hints.walkthrough: Let best(i) be the most coins using the first i stalls. For stall i you either skip it (best(i-1)) or take it, which forces you to skip stall i-1, giving prizes[i] + best(i-2). So best(i) = max(best(i-1), best(i-2) + prizes[i]). Trying every legal set of stalls by recursion is exponential. Because best(i) only needs the previous two values, you can keep just two variables: O(n) time, O(1) space.
